paragraphs.text: Two curiosities stood at the start. Rubbed amber, called elektron in Greek, attracts chaff and feathers, and the lodestone attracts iron. Greek tradition credits Thales of Miletus with noticing both around 600 BCE. By the eleventh century Chinese writers such as Shen Kuo described the magnetic compass, and in Europe it guided navigators from the twelfth century onward.

In De Magnete (1600) William Gilbert separated the two effects. With a pivoted needle, the versorium, he showed that many substances besides amber attract when rubbed, coined the Latin word electricus for them, and argued that the Earth itself is a great magnet. Electricity and magnetism entered the seventeenth century as distinct phenomena.

The mathematical frame came from mechanics. Newton's Principia (1687) describes a body by its position in Euclidean space and its state of motion, given by position together with velocity. Rates of change in time connect them, and a force is whatever changes velocity: m dv/dt = F. Forces from several sources combine by the parallelogram rule, already used by Simon Stevin in 1586. Newton's inverse-square law of gravity became the template that the electricians of the next century would imitate.

Stephen Gray showed in 1729 that the "electric virtue" could travel hundreds of feet along a packthread line but not along silk, the first clear distinction between conductors and insulators. In 1733 Charles Du Fay found two kinds of electrification, which he called vitreous and resinous: like kinds repel and unlike kinds attract.

In 1745 and 1746 Ewald von Kleist and Pieter van Musschenbroek independently found that a water-filled glass jar could store a startling amount of electricity. The Leyden jar made it possible to accumulate, carry and discharge electricity at will, and so made experiments repeatable.

Benjamin Franklin, in letters from 1747 onward, proposed a single electric fluid whose excess or deficit makes a body positive or negative. His central claim was that electrification only moves the fluid around: what one body gains, another loses. In modern terms, electric charge is a signed quantity that is additive and conserved. Charging a Leyden jar does not create charge; it separates it.

Joseph Priestley noticed in 1767 that no electric force acts on objects inside a charged hollow conductor. Newton had shown that a uniform shell exerts no gravitational force on bodies inside it, and only an inverse-square law has that property, so Priestley guessed that the electric force also falls off as 1/r². Henry Cavendish tested the idea around 1773 with concentric spheres and found the exponent to be 2 within about one part in fifty, but he never published; Maxwell edited his notes in 1879.

Charles-Augustin de Coulomb measured the force directly in 1785 with a torsion balance. The repulsion between two small charged spheres varies inversely as the square of their distance, and the same law holds between magnetic poles. The Coulomb law gives the force between any two point charges.

For many charges one needs the whole configuration of charges and their positions. The force on any one charge is the vector sum of the pairwise forces, each pair acting as though the others were absent. This principle of superposition is so natural that it was rarely stated, yet it is a strong physical claim: electrostatics is linear.

Coulomb's law said what happens between a pair. The mathematicians who had been studying Newtonian gravitation asked a different question: what is the force at each point of space due to a whole distribution of matter? Lagrange noticed in 1773 that the gravitational force is the gradient of a single scalar function. Laplace showed in the 1780s that this function satisfies ∇²V = 0 in empty space, and Poisson in 1813 added the source term inside matter, giving Poisson's equation.

Poisson brought these methods to electricity in 1812, treating charge as a continuous density spread over the surfaces of conductors. Point charges and smooth densities were later put on one footing by the delta function of Dirac (1927) and Laurent Schwartz's theory of distributions (1945), a modern convenience adopted here.

George Green, a self-taught miller from Nottingham, published his Essay in 1828. He named the scalar function the potential, proved the integral theorem now called Green's theorem, and introduced the Green's function for solving Poisson's equation with given boundary values on conductors. Because only the potential's gradient gives the force, the potential is fixed only up to an additive constant.

Mikhail Ostrogradsky (1826) and Carl Friedrich Gauss (1813, 1839) established the divergence theorem, which turns a volume integral of sources into a surface integral of flux. For electricity it says that the flux of force through a closed surface measures the charge enclosed. Combined with symmetry, it gives the force of a charged sphere or wire without any integration.

These tools make it natural to speak of the electric force per unit charge at each point, and of the whole distribution of that force over space, obtained from the potential by a gradient and recovered from it by line integrals that do not depend on the path. The work needed to assemble a distribution of charge turns out to be a quadratic form in the charges. For now the field is a calculating device: the forces themselves are still thought to act at a distance.

Luigi Galvani's experiments on frog legs (1791) led Alessandro Volta to build the first battery, a pile of zinc and copper discs announced in 1800. For the first time electricity could flow steadily. Volta described the driving "tension" of the pile, our voltage, and had earlier related a conductor's charge to its tension through its capacity, Q = CV.

A steady flow of charge is a current, and its distribution through a conductor is the current density. Georg Simon Ohm found in 1827 that the current through a wire is proportional to the tension across it, which defines the wire's resistance. In local form, Ohm's law says the current density is proportional to the electric field.

Gustav Kirchhoff stated his circuit laws in 1845: the currents entering a junction sum to zero. Its local version is the continuity equation, which expresses Franklin's conservation of charge point by point. In 1849 Kirchhoff identified Ohm's tension with a difference of Green's electrostatic potential, joining the theory of currents to the theory of static charges.

In 1820 Hans Christian Ørsted saw a compass needle swing when a nearby wire carried a current. It was the first link between electricity and magnetism, and a strange one: the needle turned to stand across the wire rather than pointing toward it.

Within months Jean-Baptiste Biot and Félix Savart measured how the magnetic action of a long straight wire falls off with distance, and Laplace distilled their results into a law for each small element of current, the Biot–Savart law. Its direction is given by a cross product, notation that Gibbs and Heaviside standardized only in the 1880s. Because a cross product depends on a choice of handedness, the magnetic field is a pseudovector.

André-Marie Ampère, starting in September 1820, measured the forces between current-carrying wires and proposed that magnets owe their power to tiny circulating currents. His 1826 memoir founded "electrodynamics". Each element of wire feels a force at right angles to both itself and the magnetic field. Ampère's law, in the circulation form that Maxwell later wrote with the curl, says that the magnetic field circulates around currents in proportion to the current enclosed.

On 29 August 1831 Michael Faraday wound two coils on an iron ring. Closing the circuit of one produced a brief current in the other, while a steady current produced nothing. Moving a magnet into a coil had the same effect. What drives the induced electromotive force is change: the rate at which the magnetic flux through the circuit changes, which Faraday pictured as the number of lines of force threading it. Emil Lenz supplied the sign in 1834: the induced current opposes the change. Together these make Faraday's law of induction.

Faraday had no formal mathematics and thought in pictures. Lines of force filled the space around magnets and charges, and he came to regard them as physically real, a condition of space itself rather than a bookkeeping device. In 1845 he found that a magnetic field rotates the plane of polarized light passing through heavy glass, and in 1846 he speculated that light might be a vibration of the lines of force.
This is the birth of the field concept in physics. The electric and magnetic fields stop being sums of distant forces and become the state of the region in which forces act.

On the continent, physicists kept to action at a distance but made it quantitative. Franz Neumann (1845) derived induced currents from a potential built from the currents in a circuit, and William Thomson (1847) represented magnetic forces through a vector function in a mechanical analogy. These are the first appearances of what Maxwell would call the electromagnetic momentum and we call the vector potential, whose curl gives the magnetic field and whose loop integral gives the flux.

Wilhelm Weber (1846) proposed a force law between moving charges and, with Rudolf Kohlrausch in 1856, measured the ratio between the electrostatic and electromagnetic units of charge. That ratio is fixed by the two couplings in the electric and magnetic force laws, and it has the units of a speed. In modern terms it is about 3.1 × 10⁸ m/s.

Meanwhile Hippolyte Fizeau (1849) and Léon Foucault (1850, 1862) had measured the speed of light on Earth, finding values near 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Kirchhoff showed in 1857 that electrical signals on an ideal wire travel at Weber's speed. The numerical match was noticed, but no theory yet explained it.

James Clerk Maxwell set out to put Faraday's pictures into mathematics. "On Faraday's Lines of Force" (1855–56) built analogies with fluid flow. "On Physical Lines of Force" (1861–62) imagined space filled with rotating molecular vortices separated by idle wheels. That mechanical model led him to an extra term in Ampère's law, the displacement current.

The term is forced by consistency. Ampère's law sets the curl of the magnetic field equal to the current, and the divergence of any curl vanishes, so the current would have to be divergence-free. But the continuity equation says the divergence of the current is minus the rate at which charge accumulates, which is not zero while a capacitor charges. Adding μ₀ε₀ ∂E/∂t restores agreement. The corrected equations admit transverse waves whose speed Maxwell computed from the Weber–Kohlrausch ratio. It matched Fizeau's speed of light, and Maxwell concluded that light is an electromagnetic disturbance.

"A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field" (1865) dropped the vortices and stated the theory as twenty equations in twenty variables, which we now write as the four Maxwell equations. The electric and magnetic fields together form a single dynamical state that evolves in time from its present values, with electrostatics as the special case in which nothing changes.

The Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism (1873) located energy in the field itself and expressed electromagnetic forces as stresses transmitted through the medium. From these stresses Maxwell predicted that light exerts a pressure on any surface it strikes.

Bernhard Riemann suggested in 1858, in a paper published only in 1867, that electrical action spreads at the speed of light. In 1867 the Danish physicist Ludvig Lorenz, independently of Maxwell, wrote the scalar and vector potentials as integrals over sources evaluated at the earlier, retarded time, under a condition that makes each potential obey the wave equation. The condition is called the Lorenz gauge and is often misattributed to H. A. Lorentz.

Potentials are not unique. Adding the gradient of any function to A, and subtracting that function's time derivative from φ, leaves the electric and magnetic fields unchanged. Maxwell, in the Treatise, chose the condition ∇·A = 0, now the Coulomb gauge, and Hermann von Helmholtz (1870) compared a whole family of choices while weighing the rival theories. Such a condition is a gauge fixing. The freedom itself, later named a gauge transformation, means that the physical content lies in the class of equivalent potentials rather than in any single pair.

That potentials exist at all is a statement about the field equations: a divergence-free field is a curl and a curl-free field is a gradient, at least in regions without holes. This is the Poincaré lemma, named for work of the 1880s although Stokes, Thomson and Maxwell already relied on it. In the decades that followed, Heaviside and Hertz regarded potentials as mathematical scaffolding to be removed from the theory.

John Henry Poynting (1884) and Oliver Heaviside (1885) independently derived the local law of energy conservation for the field, Poynting's theorem. Energy flows through space along the Poynting vector E × B / μ₀. In a circuit, energy reaches a resistor through the surrounding field rather than along the inside of the wires.

Heaviside, and Heinrich Hertz shortly after, eliminated the potentials from Maxwell's equations and rewrote them as the four vector equations in E and B used today. Josiah Willard Gibbs and Heaviside developed the vector algebra and calculus that made this compact notation possible.

Between 1886 and 1888 Hertz generated electromagnetic waves with spark-gap oscillators and detected them across his laboratory. He measured their wavelength and showed that they reflect, refract and can be polarized, just like light. Free radiation modes are naturally described by Fourier's decomposition (1822) into plane waves.

Fields carry momentum as well as energy. Henri Poincaré assigned the field a momentum density S/c² in 1900, and Pyotr Lebedev (1900) and Ernest Nichols with Gordon Hull (1901) measured the radiation pressure that Maxwell had predicted.

Maxwell's theory described continuous media. Hendrik Antoon Lorentz, from 1892, split the world into a field in empty space and discrete charged particles that act as its sources. Heaviside (1889) and Lorentz (1895) gave the force on a moving charge, F = q(E + v × B). This completes the theory: fields tell charges how to move, and charges tell fields how to change.

In 1897 J. J. Thomson deflected cathode rays with crossed electric and magnetic fields, balanced the two forces to find the particles' speed, and measured their charge-to-mass ratio; the velocity-dependent force is also how a magnetic field is probed with moving charges. Robert Millikan's oil-drop experiments, from 1909, showed that charge comes in whole multiples of the electron's charge e.

An accelerating charge radiates. Joseph Larmor (1897) gave the radiated power of a slowly moving charge, and Alfred-Marie Liénard (1898) and Emil Wiechert (1900) found the exact retarded potentials of a point charge in arbitrary motion. The same power follows from integrating the Poynting flux over a distant sphere.

Maxwell's equations predict a single speed c, but relative to what? Experiments such as Michelson and Morley's (1887) found no trace of motion through the ether. Lorentz (1904) found the transformations of space and time that leave Maxwell's equations unchanged, and Henri Poincaré (1905) showed that they form a group, the Lorentz group. Unlike rotations about a single axis, boosts in different directions do not commute.

Albert Einstein's 1905 paper "On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies" began from an electromagnetic puzzle: a magnet moving past a conductor and a conductor moving past a magnet produce the same current, yet were explained differently. Einstein took the relativity principle and the constancy of c as postulates, so that Maxwell's theory needed no change while mechanics did.

Hermann Minkowski (1908) recast the theory in four-dimensional spacetime. The potentials combine into a four-potential, charge and current into a four-current, and the electric and magnetic fields into one antisymmetric field tensor. What one observer calls electric another calls partly magnetic, but two invariants are the same for everyone. Energy density, energy flux, momentum density and stress combine into a single energy–momentum tensor.

Karl Schwarzschild (1903) derived the motion of charges and the field equations together from a single action principle. For a charge, the Lagrangian contains the term q v·A, and its Euler–Lagrange equation is the Lorentz force. A gauge transformation changes the Lagrangian only by a total time derivative, which leaves the motion unchanged.

The Legendre transform leads to the Hamiltonian description in phase space. The canonical momentum p = mv + qA shifts under gauge transformations, so it is not directly measurable; the kinetic momentum p − qA is. In terms of Poisson brackets, the components of the kinetic momentum fail to commute in a magnetic field. The field itself becomes a Hamiltonian system on its own phase space, with Gauss's law acting as a constraint, a structure Dirac made systematic around 1950.

Emmy Noether proved in 1918 that every continuous symmetry of an action yields a conservation law. Applied to electromagnetism, Noether's theorem gives conserved totals of energy, momentum and angular momentum, which balance only when the field's contributions are counted.

Hermann Weyl (1918) proposed a scale invariance he called Eichinvarianz, "gauge invariance", hoping to unify electromagnetism with gravity. Einstein objected, and the idea failed in that form. After quantum mechanics, Vladimir Fock (1926) and Fritz London (1927) saw that the right symmetry is a change of quantum phase, and Weyl (1929) recast his idea accordingly. Gauge symmetry now explains charge conservation instead of assuming it.

Élie Cartan's calculus of differential forms, developed from 1899, gives the theory its most compact statement. The exterior derivative unifies gradient, curl and divergence, and its property d² = 0 contains both curl∘grad = 0 and div∘curl = 0. The wedge product builds higher forms, and the Hodge star, developed by W. V. D. Hodge in the 1930s, carries all the metric information. Maxwell's equations become dF = 0 and d⋆F = μ₀⋆J, and charge conservation follows from d² = 0.

Paul Dirac (1931) showed that a magnetic monopole is consistent with quantum mechanics only if the potentials live on overlapping patches glued together by gauge transformations. The global object is a principal U(1) bundle whose connection is the potential and whose curvature is the field. Because U(1) is commutative, the curvature has no quadratic term, and the theory stays linear. Chen Ning Yang and Robert Mills (1954) generalized the construction to non-commutative groups.

Werner Ehrenberg and Raymond Siday (1949) and, independently, Yakir Aharonov and David Bohm (1959) predicted that electrons passing on either side of a shielded solenoid, where B = 0, acquire a phase difference set by the holonomy ∮A·dl. Robert Chambers observed the effect in 1960, and Akira Tonomura's group confirmed it decisively in 1986. Tai Tsun Wu and Yang (1975) wrote out the dictionary between gauge physics and fibre-bundle geometry. Classical electromagnetism had turned out to be the simplest gauge theory, the model on which the forces of particle physics are built.

By 1900 the classical theory looked complete, yet it failed on the light emitted by hot bodies. Kirchhoff (1859) showed that the radiation inside a cavity at temperature T has a universal spectrum, and by 1900 Otto Lummer, Ernst Pringsheim, Heinrich Rubens and Ferdinand Kurlbaum had measured it precisely. Classical physics makes a definite prediction: treat each radiation mode as an oscillator and give it the average energy kT required by the equipartition theorem. The result, worked out by Rayleigh (1900) and Jeans (1905), agrees at long wavelengths but makes the energy grow without bound at short ones, what Ehrenfest later called the ultraviolet catastrophe.

Max Planck found a formula that fits the data in October 1900 and, in December, derived it by assuming that oscillators exchange energy with radiation only in packets E = hν. The Planck relation introduced a new constant of nature, Planck's constant, and with it the correct spectrum. Planck regarded the packets as a feature of emission and absorption, not of light itself.

Einstein went further in 1905: light itself comes in quanta. This explained the photoelectric effect, in which the energy of ejected electrons depends on the light's frequency rather than its intensity, contrary to the classical wave picture. Millikan confirmed Einstein's equation in 1916, and Arthur Compton's 1923 X-ray scattering experiments showed that the light quantum, named the photon by Gilbert Lewis in 1926, carries momentum h/λ as well as energy.

Atoms posed a second crisis. Rutherford's 1911 nuclear atom has electrons orbiting a tiny nucleus, but an accelerating charge radiates, so by Larmor's formula a classical atom should collapse in about 10⁻¹¹ s while emitting a continuous spectrum. Real atoms are stable and emit sharp spectral lines, whose hydrogen series Balmer (1885) and Rydberg (1888) had already fitted. Niels Bohr (1913) postulated stationary orbits with quantized angular momentum, the atom emitting a quantum hν only when it jumps between them. The rules worked for hydrogen but were an uneasy patchwork of classical orbits and quantum conditions.

Louis de Broglie proposed in 1924 that matter also has wave properties, with wavelength h/p. In 1925 Werner Heisenberg rebuilt atomic physics from arrays of transition quantities, which Max Born and Pascual Jordan recognized as matrices that do not commute. They found the rule xp − px = iħ, where ħ = h/2π.

Paul Dirac, reading Heisenberg's paper, noticed that the commutator of two quantum quantities behaves exactly like the Poisson bracket of the corresponding classical ones: both are bilinear, antisymmetric and satisfy the Jacobi identity. His rule replaces {A, B} by [Â, B̂]/iħ. This canonical commutation relation is the heart of the move from classical to quantum: the commutative algebra of functions on phase space becomes a non-commutative algebra of operators.

Erwin Schrödinger (1926) wrote a wave equation for de Broglie's waves, the Schrödinger equation, and showed that it reproduces Heisenberg's results. The state of a system is no longer a point (x, p) in phase space but a vector in a Hilbert space, a structure John von Neumann made rigorous in 1932. Hydrogen's energy levels now follow from an eigenvalue problem, without Bohr's ad hoc orbits.

Max Born (1926) supplied the interpretation: the wave function gives probabilities. The Born rule turns the state into the statistics of measurement outcomes. Paul Ehrenfest (1927) showed that expectation values of position and momentum obey Newton's laws when the force varies slowly across the wave packet, which is how classical mechanics reappears as a limit.

To put a charge in an electromagnetic field, quantum mechanics takes the classical Hamiltonian H = (p − qA)²/2m + qφ and replaces p by the operator −iħ∇. With this minimal coupling, the potentials themselves, not only E and B, enter the Schrödinger equation. A gauge transformation of the potentials must then be accompanied by a change of the wave function's phase, ψ → e^{iqχ/ħ}ψ: Weyl's idea of 1929 at work.

In a magnetic field the kinetic momenta do not commute, just as their Poisson brackets did not. Lev Landau showed in 1930 that an electron's motion in a uniform field is quantized into Landau levels spaced by ħ times the cyclotron frequency. The quantum Hall effect, discovered by Klaus von Klitzing in 1980, is a striking consequence.

The holonomy of the classical potential becomes measurable. An electron wave split around a solenoid recombines with a relative phase q∮A·dl/ħ, shifting the interference pattern although the electron never enters the region where B is non-zero. This is the Aharonov–Bohm effect of Part I, now seen from the quantum side.

Schrödinger's equation is not relativistic, and electrons have spin, revealed by Otto Stern and Walther Gerlach (1922) and described by Wolfgang Pauli (1927) with two-component wave functions. In 1928 Dirac found a first-order relativistic equation by taking a square root of the relativistic energy relation. It requires matrices γ^μ obeying the anticommutation rules of a Clifford algebra. The Dirac equation, with minimal coupling built in, is Lorentz-covariant.

Its solutions are four-component spinors, which transform under a double cover of the Lorentz group. Spin emerges automatically, together with a magnetic moment whose g-factor is exactly 2 and the fine structure of hydrogen's lines.

The equation also has negative-energy solutions. Dirac first imagined them filled by a sea of electrons and in 1931 predicted that a hole in the sea would be a particle with the electron's mass and opposite charge. Carl Anderson found the positron in cosmic rays in 1932. Particles can be created and destroyed in pairs, so a theory with a fixed number of particles cannot be the whole story.

Field quantization began with the 1925–26 "three-man paper" of Born, Heisenberg and Jordan. Each classical radiation mode is a harmonic oscillator, and quantizing it with the canonical commutator gives creation and annihilation operators that add or remove one quantum of energy ħω. The quanta of the electromagnetic field are photons: Einstein's light quanta follow from Maxwell's theory plus quantization.

Dirac's 1927 paper on the emission and absorption of radiation treated the field and an atom together. The states of the field live in Fock space (Vladimir Fock, 1932), which contains any number of photons. Even with no photons present the field fluctuates, and these fluctuations drive spontaneous emission, explaining the coefficient Einstein had introduced in 1917.

Enrico Fermi (1932) wrote the quantized potentials as field operators in the Coulomb gauge, the form used in most early calculations. Roy Glauber (1963) showed that coherent states with many photons behave exactly like classical Maxwell fields. The vacuum's zero-point energy has measurable effects: Hendrik Casimir predicted in 1948 that two uncharged parallel conducting plates attract, because they restrict the modes between them, and the Casimir force was measured precisely by Steven Lamoreaux in 1997.

Heisenberg and Pauli (1929) formulated a general quantum field theory in which the electron, like the photon, is the quantum of a field. The electron–positron field obeys anticommutation relations, which encode Pauli's exclusion principle (Jordan and Wigner, 1928).

The strength of the interaction is set by the fine-structure constant α = e²/4πε₀ħc ≈ 1/137, introduced by Arnold Sommerfeld in 1916. It is a pure number combining the charge, the classical coupling ε₀, the speed of light and Planck's constant. Because α is small, calculations proceed by perturbation theory as a power series in α.

First-order results were excellent, for example the Klein–Nishina formula (1929) for Compton scattering. Higher orders gave infinities. J. Robert Oppenheimer (1930) found that the electron's interaction with its own field shifts its energy by an infinite amount, and Victor Weisskopf (1934, 1939) showed the divergence to be milder than the classical one but still present. For nearly two decades the infinities stalled QED.

Experiment forced the issue. In 1947 Willis Lamb and Robert Retherford found that two hydrogen levels which the Dirac equation predicts to be exactly degenerate are split by about 1000 MHz (about 1058 MHz in later, more precise measurements), the Lamb shift. In the same year Polykarp Kusch and Henry Foley measured an anomalous magnetic moment: the electron's g-factor is slightly larger than Dirac's 2.

Hans Bethe (1947) estimated the Lamb shift on a train ride by subtracting the infinite self-energy of a free electron from that of a bound one, and found about 1040 MHz. The idea became renormalization: the infinities are absorbed into the electron's measured mass and charge, and predictions are expressed in terms of those measured values.

Sin-Itiro Tomonaga, Julian Schwinger and Richard Feynman built fully relativistic versions of the theory. Feynman's route started from the classical action: in the path integral (1948) every possible history contributes a phase e^{iS/ħ}, and the classical path dominates when the action is large compared with ħ. Feynman's diagrams organize the perturbation series as pictures of photons and electrons being emitted and absorbed.

Freeman Dyson (1949) proved the approaches equivalent and showed that QED is renormalizable: a finite number of measured quantities absorbs all the infinities, to every order. The theory is packaged in the S-matrix of transition amplitudes, from which cross sections follow. Schwinger (1948) obtained the anomalous moment α/2π ≈ 0.00116, matching Kusch and Foley, and the Lamb shift came out right.

Renormalization also changes the meaning of charge. Virtual electron–positron pairs screen a charge, so the effective coupling grows at short distances, the vacuum polarization computed by Edwin Uehling in 1935. Murray Gell-Mann and Francis Low (1954) described how the coupling runs with energy; at the mass of the Z boson α is measured to be about 1/128.

The modern view starts from symmetry. Require the theory to be unchanged when the electron field's phase is changed independently at every point, ψ → e^{iqχ(x)/ħ}ψ. Derivatives of ψ then pick up unwanted terms unless they are replaced by covariant derivatives containing a potential, and that potential must transform exactly as the electromagnetic gauge transformation does. The local gauge principle turns Part I's U(1) connection into the coupling between light and matter.

The result is the QED Lagrangian: the Dirac term for the electron with its covariant derivative, plus the Maxwell term for the photon. Feynman's rules follow from it directly. John Ward (1950) and Yasushi Takahashi (1957) derived the identities that express gauge invariance among the amplitudes; they keep the photon massless and make charge renormalization the same for every charged particle.

Yang and Mills (1954) extended the gauge principle to non-commutative groups, the route to the electroweak theory and quantum chromodynamics; QED remains the abelian case. Its predictions are among the most precisely tested in science: the electron's anomalous magnetic moment, computed through fifth order in α, agrees with measurement to roughly a part in a trillion in g. Maxwell's equations survive as the classical limit of a quantum field, recovered when photon numbers are large.

nodes.label: Force on a charge
nodes.description: Measured from a body's acceleration (F = ma) or by balancing it against a known force. Every force law in the story predicts it, so more and more alternative routes lead here.

nodes.label: Position
nodes.description: Where a body sits in Euclidean 3-space, measured with rulers. Separations r = x − x′ enter every force law. A primitive geometric observable.

nodes.label: Velocity
nodes.description: v = dx/dt from successive position measurements. It becomes essential once magnetic forces turn out to depend on motion.

nodes.label: Particle state of motion
nodes.description: Position and velocity together: Newton's description of a body's state.
nodes.math_structure: Point of the tangent bundle Tℝ³; over time, a curve x(t).

nodes.label: Vector addition
nodes.description: How forces and fields combine. Because order and grouping do not matter, the total force from any number of sources is well defined.

nodes.label: Time derivative
nodes.description: Generates time evolution. Its commuting with spatial derivatives is used when the curl equations are combined into wave equations.

nodes.label: Electric charge
nodes.description: A signed scalar property of bodies, inferred from the forces they exert on one another. Experimentally additive and conserved, and (Millikan) quantized in units of e.

nodes.label: Additivity and conservation of charge
nodes.description: Franklin's principle: charges add with sign, and electrification only moves charge from one body to another. A global statement that the continuity equation later makes local.

nodes.label: Coulomb law
nodes.description: k q₁q₂ r̂/r² with k = 1/4πε₀. Exchange symmetry gives Newton's third law; the inverse-square form is exactly what makes Gauss's law hold.

nodes.label: Point-charge configuration
nodes.description: The simplest state of an electrostatic system: which charges there are and where they sit.
nodes.math_structure: A point in ℝ³ᴺ with a charge label qᵢ on each of N points.

nodes.label: Superposition
nodes.description: The map from sources to forces and fields is linear: contributions from separate sources simply add. Exact in vacuum Maxwell theory.

nodes.label: Poisson's equation
nodes.description: ∇²φ = −ρ/ε₀. Linearity means solutions superpose; uniqueness means sources plus boundary data fully determine the state.

nodes.label: Charge density
nodes.description: Charge per unit volume. Smooth densities and point charges (via δ functions) are elements of the same space.
nodes.math_structure: Scalar distribution (signed measure) on ℝ³.

nodes.label: Delta function
nodes.description: Lets point charges and smooth densities live in one space: ρ = Σ qᵢ δ³(x − xᵢ). Introduced by Dirac (1927) and made rigorous by Schwartz (1945).

nodes.label: Potential up to a constant
nodes.description: The electrostatic state written as one scalar function, with its built-in redundancy made explicit.
nodes.math_structure: Element of the quotient C^∞(ℝ³)/ℝ: an equivalence class of functions differing by constants.

nodes.label: Boundary values
nodes.description: The part of the state fixed by conductors and the outside world. Needed to make Poisson's problem well posed.
nodes.math_structure: Values φ|∂Ω (Dirichlet) or ∂φ/∂n (Neumann) on boundary surfaces.

nodes.label: Gradient
nodes.description: Because ∇ kills constants, φ and φ + c give the same force. This is the first redundancy (gauge freedom) in the description of the state.

nodes.label: Divergence theorem
nodes.description: Converts local statements about sources into statements about flux through surfaces, and back. Also used for any flux integral.

nodes.label: Electric flux
nodes.description: Φ_E = ∮E·dA through a closed surface. Gauss's law says it equals Q_enc/ε₀ however the enclosed charges are arranged.

nodes.label: Symmetry arguments
nodes.description: If a source distribution is unchanged by rotations, translations or reflections, the field it produces must transform the same way. With Gauss's or Ampère's law this fixes fields without integrating.

nodes.label: Electric field value
nodes.description: Operationally E = lim F/q for a small test charge at rest: a derived observable built from force and charge measurements.

nodes.label: Electric field
nodes.description: The whole field as one object, a function on space. A calculating device for Green and Gauss; a physical state for Faraday and Maxwell.
nodes.math_structure: Vector field ℝ³ → ℝ³ (curl-free in statics).

nodes.label: Line integrals
nodes.description: Integrals along curves. Path independence holds for curl-free fields on regions without holes; the exception returns with holonomy in the final section.

nodes.label: Electrostatic energy
nodes.description: Work needed to assemble a configuration from charges far apart. Measured through work done or heat released on discharge.

nodes.label: Quadratic energy form
nodes.description: U(E₁ + E₂) = U(E₁) + U(E₂) + a cross term. The cross term is why energies do not simply add even though fields do.

nodes.label: Voltage
nodes.description: Volta's tension, a potential difference φ(b) − φ(a): what a voltmeter reads. Invariant under φ → φ + const, which is why it is measurable while φ itself is not.

nodes.label: Capacitance
nodes.description: C = Q/ΔV for a conductor or pair of conductors. Depends only on geometry (and the medium) because electrostatics is linear.

nodes.label: Current
nodes.description: I = dQ/dt through a surface, read by an ammeter. Equal to the flux of the current density.

nodes.label: Current density
nodes.description: Charge flux per unit area. Together with ρ it specifies all the sources of the field.
nodes.math_structure: Vector field J(x, t); in steady flow ∇·J = 0.

nodes.label: Resistance
nodes.description: R = ΔV/I for a conductor. Ohm found it independent of the current for a given wire at fixed temperature.

nodes.label: Ohm's law
nodes.description: J = σE inside a conductor, or ΔV = IR for a whole wire. Unlike Maxwell's equations it describes a material, valid for many conductors at moderate fields.

nodes.label: Continuity equation
nodes.description: Charge cannot vanish in one place and reappear in another: change inside a volume equals flux through its boundary. Later developments derive it rather than assume it.

nodes.label: Magnetic field value
nodes.description: The magnetic action at a point, read with a compass or a probe coil, or inferred from the velocity-dependent force on a moving charge.

nodes.label: Biot–Savart law
nodes.description: Field of a current element, (μ₀/4π) I dl × r̂/r². The magnetic counterpart of the Coulomb law.

nodes.label: Cross product
nodes.description: a×b = −b×a, and a×(b×c) ≠ (a×b)×c. Its dependence on handedness makes B a pseudovector, and since v×B ⟂ v, magnetic forces do no work.

nodes.label: Curl and Stokes' theorem
nodes.description: Measures circulation. The identity div∘curl = 0 is what later forces the displacement current.

nodes.label: Magnetic field
nodes.description: The magnetic field as a single object on space.
nodes.math_structure: Divergence-free pseudovector field on ℝ³.

nodes.label: Electromotive force
nodes.description: ℰ = ∮(E + v×B)·dl around a circuit, measured as the voltage across a small gap in the loop.

nodes.label: Magnetic flux
nodes.description: Φ_B = ∫B·dA through a surface bounded by a loop: Faraday's count of lines of force threading a circuit.

nodes.label: Faraday's law
nodes.description: A changing magnetic flux induces a circulating electric field; the minus sign makes induced currents oppose the change.

nodes.label: Vector potential
nodes.description: Neumann's and Thomson's potential, Maxwell's electromagnetic momentum. Useful for calculation; not observable by itself.
nodes.math_structure: Vector field A(x, t) whose curl is B: one representative of a gauge class.

nodes.label: Couplings ε₀ and μ₀
nodes.description: Fix the strength of electric forces between charges and magnetic forces between currents. 1/√(ε₀μ₀) is the speed Weber and Kohlrausch found as a ratio of units. (In the 2019 SI they are fixed through the measured fine-structure constant.)

nodes.label: Speed of light
nodes.description: Measured astronomically (Rømer 1676, Bradley 1729) and on Earth by Fizeau (1849). After Maxwell it is also predicted from ε₀ and μ₀. Only the prediction is drawn as a route; the measurements are not.

nodes.label: Maxwell's equations
nodes.description: The complete field law. Gauss's two laws constrain each moment; Faraday's and the Ampère–Maxwell law evolve it.

nodes.label: Dynamical field state
nodes.description: Electric and magnetic fields as one state that evolves in time.
nodes.math_structure: Pair of vector fields with ∇·E = ρ/ε₀ and ∇·B = 0 at one time: Cauchy data.

nodes.label: Field energy density
nodes.description: u = ½(ε₀|E|² + |B|²/μ₀). Integrates to the total energy stored in the field.

nodes.label: Maxwell stress tensor
nodes.description: Expresses the force on charges inside a volume as a surface integral over the field around them.

nodes.label: Wave operator
nodes.description: □ = c⁻²∂²/∂t² − ∇². Choosing the retarded Green's function means influences travel at c from the past.

nodes.label: Gauge fixing
nodes.description: A rule that picks one pair (φ, A) from each class, chosen to simplify the equations.

nodes.label: Gauge transformations
nodes.description: (φ, A) → (φ − ∂χ/∂t, A + ∇χ). Two transformations compose in either order to χ₁ + χ₂: the group is commutative.

nodes.label: Gauge class of potentials
nodes.description: The physical state in the potential description. Everything observable is a function of these classes.
nodes.math_structure: Orbit of the gauge group in the space of pairs (φ, A): a point of a quotient space.

nodes.label: Poincaré lemma
nodes.description: ∇·B = 0 ⇒ B = ∇×A, and ∇×(E + ∂A/∂t) = 0 ⇒ E + ∂A/∂t = −∇φ. It can fail on regions with holes, which is where holonomy lives.

nodes.label: Poynting's theorem
nodes.description: ∂u/∂t + ∇·S = −J·E: field energy changes by flowing away or by doing work on charges.

nodes.label: Poynting vector
nodes.description: S = E×B/μ₀, the energy flux in W/m². Its time average is the intensity a detector measures.

nodes.label: Wave data
nodes.description: Wavelength, frequency and polarization, measured with standing waves, interferometers and polarizers. In vacuum ω = c|k| and k ⟂ E ⟂ B.

nodes.label: Radiation modes
nodes.description: The source-free field described by its modes rather than by its values at points.
nodes.math_structure: Amplitudes a(k, λ) for wave vectors k and two transverse polarizations λ.

nodes.label: Fourier decomposition
nodes.description: Writes any field as a superposition of plane waves e^{i(k·x − ωt)}, in which the field equations become algebraic.

nodes.label: Field momentum density
nodes.description: g = S/c². Observed as radiation pressure on mirrors and absorbers.

nodes.label: Radiated power
nodes.description: Energy per unit time leaving an accelerating charge through a distant sphere.

nodes.label: Lorentz group
nodes.description: Two non-parallel boosts compose to a boost plus a rotation (the Wigner rotation). Under boosts, E and B mix.

nodes.label: Four-potential
nodes.description: Scalar and vector potentials as a single spacetime object.
nodes.math_structure: 1-form A on Minkowski spacetime with components (φ/c, A).

nodes.label: Four-current
nodes.description: Charge and current density as a single spacetime object.
nodes.math_structure: Vector field on spacetime (cρ, J), equivalently the 3-form ⋆J.

nodes.label: Field tensor
nodes.description: Electric and magnetic fields as one observer-independent object.
nodes.math_structure: Antisymmetric rank-2 tensor (2-form) on spacetime; F₀ᵢ ∝ Eᵢ/c, Fᵢⱼ ∝ εᵢⱼₖBₖ.

nodes.label: Lorentz invariants
nodes.description: E·B and |E|² − c²|B|² take the same value for every inertial observer. If E ⟂ B and |E| < c|B|, some frame sees a purely magnetic field.

nodes.label: Energy–momentum tensor
nodes.description: One symmetric tensor whose components, for a given observer, are the energy density, Poynting flux, momentum density and Maxwell stress.

nodes.label: Action principle
nodes.description: Under a gauge change L shifts by q dχ/dt, a total time derivative, so the equations of motion are unchanged.
properties: L defined up to a total derivative

nodes.label: Legendre transform
nodes.description: Moves from the velocity description to the momentum description: p = ∂L/∂v, H = p·v − L.

nodes.label: Particle phase space
nodes.description: The Hamiltonian state of a charge. Using kinetic momenta as coordinates instead puts the magnetic field into the symplectic form.
nodes.math_structure: Cotangent bundle T*ℝ³ with symplectic form ω = dp∧dx.

nodes.label: Kinetic momentum
nodes.description: π = mv = p − qA. Gauge-invariant and measurable, for example from the curvature of a particle track. The canonical momentum p is not.

nodes.label: Poisson bracket
nodes.description: dF/dt = {F, H}. In a magnetic field the kinetic momenta do not commute: a classical non-commutativity that becomes Landau levels in quantum mechanics.

nodes.label: Field phase space
nodes.description: The field as a constrained Hamiltonian system. Gauss's law generates the gauge transformations.
nodes.math_structure: Canonical pairs (A, Π = −ε₀E) with Gauss's law as a constraint, reduced by gauge orbits.

nodes.label: Noether's theorem
nodes.description: Every continuous symmetry of the action yields a conservation law.

nodes.label: Conserved totals
nodes.description: Total energy, momentum and angular momentum of matter plus field. Conservation holds only when the field's contributions are included.

nodes.label: Exterior derivative
nodes.description: Unifies grad, curl and div. d² = 0 contains both curl∘grad = 0 and div∘curl = 0.

nodes.label: Wedge product
nodes.description: α∧β = (−1)^{pq} β∧α: 1-forms anticommute, 2-forms commute. F∧F is a 4-form proportional to E·B.

nodes.label: Hodge star
nodes.description: Carries all metric (and constitutive) information. In form language it is the only place c and spacetime geometry enter Maxwell's equations.

nodes.label: U(1) bundle
nodes.description: The global geometric state. It can carry information, such as holonomy around holes, that no single local potential captures.
nodes.math_structure: Principal U(1)-bundle over spacetime with a connection 1-form; potentials are its local expressions.

nodes.label: U(1) connection
nodes.description: In a non-abelian (Yang–Mills) theory the curvature is dA + A∧A. Electromagnetism's commutative group keeps it linear.

nodes.label: Holonomy
nodes.description: ∮A·dl around a closed loop: gauge-invariant and equal to the enclosed flux. Around a solenoid it is non-zero on loops where B = 0. With ħ, the phase exp(iq∮A·dl/ħ) is the Aharonov–Bohm phase.

nodes.label: Blackbody spectrum
nodes.description: Energy density of cavity radiation per unit frequency at temperature T, measured with bolometers around 1900. It has a peak and falls at high frequency, which classical physics cannot reproduce.

nodes.label: Equipartition theorem
nodes.description: Classical statistical mechanics gives every oscillator mean energy kT. Applied to infinitely many radiation modes, it gives infinite energy.
properties: ½kT per quadratic degree of freedom

nodes.label: Planck relation
nodes.description: The first quantum rule. It ties a frequency, a wave property, to an energy, a particle property.
properties: links particle energy to wave frequency

nodes.label: Planck's constant
nodes.description: h ≈ 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, with ħ = h/2π. The quantum of action; classical physics is the regime where actions are large compared with ħ. Exact by definition in the 2019 SI.

nodes.label: Photoelectric effect
nodes.description: Maximum kinetic energy of electrons ejected by light. It rises linearly with frequency above a threshold and does not depend on intensity.

nodes.label: Photon
nodes.description: A quantum of the electromagnetic field, with energy ħω and momentum ħk. Detected one at a time by photomultipliers and in Compton scattering.

nodes.label: Spectral lines
nodes.description: Sharp wavelengths emitted or absorbed by atoms. Hydrogen's lines fit 1/λ = R(1/m² − 1/n²).

nodes.label: Bohr orbits
nodes.description: The old quantum theory's hybrid state: classical orbits with quantum selection rules. Superseded by quantum mechanics but historically the bridge.
nodes.math_structure: Discrete set of classical orbits labelled by n, with angular momentum nħ.

nodes.label: Canonical commutator
nodes.description: Shares every algebraic property of the Poisson bracket, which is why Dirac could map one to the other. Its non-zero value iħ is the quantum.

nodes.label: Operator algebra
nodes.description: Observables become operators on states. Position and momentum no longer commute, so they cannot both be sharp: Heisenberg's uncertainty relation.

nodes.label: Schrödinger equation
nodes.description: iħ ∂ψ/∂t = Ĥψ. Linearity means quantum states superpose, the quantum descendant of the superposition principle of Part I.

nodes.label: Hilbert-space state
nodes.description: Replaces the point in phase space. It assigns amplitudes, not definite values, to every observable.
nodes.math_structure: Unit ray in a complex Hilbert space (a vector up to an overall phase).

nodes.label: Born rule
nodes.description: Connects the abstract state to what detectors record: frequencies of outcomes over many runs.

nodes.label: Outcome statistics
nodes.description: Probabilities and averages of measurement results over many identically prepared systems.

nodes.label: Minimal coupling
nodes.description: The quantum version of the classical kinetic momentum. It makes the potentials, not only the fields, act on charged quantum particles.

nodes.label: Landau levels
nodes.description: Discrete energies of a charge in a uniform magnetic field, seen in cyclotron resonance and the quantum Hall effect.

nodes.label: Aharonov–Bohm shift
nodes.description: Shift of an interference pattern by qΦ_B/ħ for electrons passing around a region of magnetic flux they never enter.

nodes.label: Clifford algebra
nodes.description: The algebra needed to take a square root of p² − m²c². Its anticommutation, not commutation, is what produces spin ½.

nodes.label: Dirac equation
nodes.description: The relativistic wave equation of the electron, the matter half of QED.

nodes.label: Dirac spinor
nodes.description: A spinor changes sign under a full 360° rotation, something no classical vector field does.
nodes.math_structure: 4-component field transforming under SL(2,ℂ), the double cover of the Lorentz group.

nodes.label: Electron g-factor
nodes.description: Ratio of the electron's magnetic moment to its spin in natural units. Dirac predicted exactly 2.

nodes.label: Positron
nodes.description: The electron's antiparticle, same mass, opposite charge. Electron–positron pairs are created and annihilated.

nodes.label: Creation and annihilation operators
nodes.description: Quantizing each field mode as an oscillator. Commutators give bosons (photons); anticommutators give fermions (electrons).
properties: raise or lower quanta by one

nodes.label: Fock space
nodes.description: The state space of a quantum field, in which particle number can change.
nodes.math_structure: Direct sum of n-particle Hilbert spaces, n = 0, 1, 2, …; basis labelled by occupation numbers.

nodes.label: Field operator
nodes.description: The quantized electromagnetic potential. Its expectation values in coherent states are classical fields.
nodes.math_structure: Operator-valued distribution on Fock space (Coulomb gauge: transverse components only).

nodes.label: Spontaneous emission rate
nodes.description: Rate at which an excited atom emits a photon with no field present, set by vacuum fluctuations.

nodes.label: Casimir force
nodes.description: Attraction between uncharged parallel plates due to the change in zero-point energy of the field modes between them.

nodes.label: Electron–positron field
nodes.description: The electron as the quantum of a field. It annihilates electrons and creates positrons.
nodes.math_structure: Anticommuting operator-valued spinor field on Fock space.

nodes.label: Fine-structure constant
nodes.description: α = e²/4πε₀ħc ≈ 1/137.036, the dimensionless strength of electromagnetism. Measured from the electron's g-factor and from atom-recoil experiments.

nodes.label: Perturbation series
nodes.description: Expands amplitudes in powers of the small coupling α. Each higher order involves more virtual particles.

nodes.label: Lamb shift
nodes.description: Splitting between hydrogen's 2S½ and 2P½ levels: about 1000 MHz in Lamb and Retherford's 1947 measurement, about 1058 MHz in later, more precise measurements.

nodes.label: Anomalous magnetic moment
nodes.description: a_e = (g − 2)/2 ≈ 0.00115965, measured by Kusch and Foley (1947) and today to about a tenth of a part per billion.

nodes.label: Renormalization
nodes.description: Expresses predictions in terms of measured quantities, so that infinities cancel. Later understood through the renormalization group.
properties: absorbs divergences into measured m and e

nodes.label: Path integral
nodes.description: Quantizes using the classical action directly, so the action principle of Part I becomes the core of quantum theory.

nodes.label: Feynman diagrams
nodes.description: Pictorial rules for the terms of the perturbation series.

nodes.label: S-matrix
nodes.description: Packages everything that can be measured in a scattering experiment.
nodes.math_structure: Unitary operator on Fock space mapping incoming to outgoing states.

nodes.label: Cross sections
nodes.description: Scattering rates per unit flux, measured in collision experiments (Compton, Møller, Bhabha scattering).

nodes.label: Running coupling
nodes.description: The effective strength of electromagnetism at momentum transfer Q, measured at colliders: about 1/128 at the Z mass.

nodes.label: Local gauge principle
nodes.description: Demanding local phase invariance requires a connection, the electromagnetic potential, and fixes how it couples to charge.

nodes.label: QED Lagrangian
nodes.description: The complete specification of quantum electrodynamics in one line: Dirac field plus Maxwell field, coupled through the covariant derivative.

nodes.label: Ward–Takahashi identities
nodes.description: Relations among amplitudes implied by gauge symmetry; they protect the theory's consistency through renormalization.

routes.title: Newton's second law
routes.formula: m dv/dt = F, dx/dt = v, integrated forward in time.

routes.title: Read off velocity
routes.formula: v = dx/dt.

inputs.role: Velocity component of the state of motion.

routes.title: Position along a trajectory
routes.formula: The position component of the state of motion.

inputs.role: Supplies x(t) at the moment of measurement.

routes.title: Read positions off the configuration
routes.formula: A coordinate of the configuration is a position measurement.

inputs.role: Each configuration lists where every charge is.

routes.title: Coulomb force sum
routes.formula: Fᵢ = Σⱼ k qᵢqⱼ(xᵢ − xⱼ)/|xᵢ − xⱼ|³.

inputs.role: Every pair of charges and their separation vectors.
The force each pair exerts on the other.
Adds the pairwise forces; commutativity and associativity make the sum independent of ordering.

routes.title: Point charges as a density
routes.formula: ρ(x) = Σ qᵢ δ³(x − xᵢ).

inputs.role: The discrete charges qᵢ at points xᵢ.
Turns each point charge into a density spike, so points and continua share one description.

routes.title: Total charge from density
routes.formula: Q = ∫ρ dV.

inputs.role: Additivity: the charge of a region is the sum (integral) of its parts.

routes.title: Test-charge definition
routes.formula: E = lim F/q as q → 0.

inputs.role: Force measured on a small test charge at rest.
The test charge; dividing removes the dependence on the probe.

routes.title: Evaluate the field at a point
routes.formula: The observable E(x₀) is the state E(·) evaluated at x₀.

inputs.role: The point at which it is read.
Field of a unit point source.
The total field is the integral of point-source fields.

routes.title: Gauss's law with symmetry
routes.formula: Avoids integration when symmetry fixes the field's shape.

inputs.role: Must be highly symmetric (sphere, line, plane).
∮E·dA = Q_enc/ε₀ links field and enclosed charge.
Makes |E| constant on a chosen surface so the integral can be inverted.
Any representative of the potential class.
The constant ambiguity drops out because ∇(const) = 0.

routes.title: Static limit of the dynamical field
routes.formula: With ∂/∂t = 0 the electric part decouples and is curl-free.

inputs.role: Set all time derivatives to zero.

routes.title: Direct flux integral
routes.formula: Φ_E = ∮E·dA.

inputs.role: The field to integrate over the surface.

routes.title: Gauss's law
routes.formula: Φ_E = Q_enc/ε₀.

routes.title: Potential from a line integral
routes.formula: φ(x) = −∫E·dl from an arbitrary reference point.

inputs.role: A curl-free field, so the integral is path-independent.
The integral; moving the reference point shifts φ by a constant.

routes.title: Solve Poisson's equation
routes.formula: ∇²φ = −ρ/ε₀ with boundary conditions.

inputs.role: Linear elliptic equation solved with a Green's function.
Boundary values make the solution unique.

routes.title: Static limit of the gauge potential
routes.formula: For static fields in Coulomb gauge, the scalar part of the representative is the electrostatic potential.

inputs.role: Fixes a representative in which φ is time-independent.

routes.title: Energy as charge times potential
routes.formula: U = ½∫ρφ dV.

inputs.role: The ½ corrects for counting each pair twice.

routes.title: Energy stored in the field
routes.formula: U = (ε₀/2)∫|E|² dV.

inputs.role: Positive-definite quadratic form in the field.

routes.title: Difference of potential values
routes.formula: ΔV = φ(b) − φ(a); the arbitrary constant cancels.

routes.title: Line integral of the field
routes.formula: ΔV = −∫ₐᵇ E·dl, path-independent in statics.

routes.title: Capacitance
routes.formula: C = Q/ΔV; linearity makes the ratio independent of Q.

inputs.role: Conductor geometry, which fixes the ratio.

routes.title: Current as flux of J
routes.formula: I = ∫J·dA.

routes.title: Resistance from voltage and current
routes.formula: R = ΔV/I.

routes.title: Local Ohm's law
routes.formula: J = σE inside a conductor.

routes.title: Density evolves by continuity
routes.formula: ∂ρ/∂t = −∇·J updates ρ in time.

inputs.role: Flux of charge out of each region.
Converts outflow into a decrease of density.

routes.title: Biot–Savart integral
routes.formula: B(x) = (μ₀/4π)∫J × (x − x′)/|x − x′|³ d³x′.

routes.title: Ampère's law with symmetry
routes.formula: ∮B·dl = μ₀I_enc.

routes.title: Evaluate the field at a point
routes.formula: B(x₀) from the field B(·).

routes.title: Infer B from the velocity-dependent force
routes.formula: Solve F − qE = q v×B for B using several velocities.

inputs.role: Total force on a moving test charge.
Inverting the cross product needs at least two independent velocities.

routes.title: Force on a current element
routes.formula: dF = I dl × B (Ampère, Laplace).

inputs.role: Makes the force perpendicular to both wire and field.

routes.title: Flux integral of B
routes.formula: Φ_B = ∫B·dA; any surface with the same boundary gives the same answer because ∇·B = 0.

routes.title: Flux from the loop integral of A
routes.formula: Φ_B = ∮A·dl by Stokes' theorem.

routes.title: Faraday's flux rule
routes.formula: ℰ = −dΦ_B/dt.

inputs.role: Supplies the law and Lenz's sign.

routes.title: Direct loop integral
routes.formula: ℰ = ∮(E + v×B)·dl.

routes.title: Measure the couplings
routes.formula: ε₀ from the strength of electric forces, μ₀ from forces between currents.

routes.title: Displacement current
routes.formula: Adding μ₀ε₀∂E/∂t to Ampère's law restores consistency with charge conservation.

inputs.role: ∇·(∇×B) = 0 would force ∇·J = 0: the contradiction to repair.

routes.title: Maxwell's equations as forms
routes.formula: dF = 0 and d⋆F = μ₀⋆J.

inputs.role: d⋆F = μ₀⋆J packages Gauss and Ampère–Maxwell; ⋆ supplies the metric.

routes.title: Predicted wave speed
routes.formula: Combining the curl equations gives wave equations with speed 1/√(μ₀ε₀).

inputs.role: Steps the state forward in time.

routes.title: Fields from potentials
routes.formula: E = −∇φ − ∂A/∂t, B = ∇×A, the same for every member of the gauge class.

routes.title: Split F by an observer
routes.formula: E and B are the components of F relative to an observer's four-velocity.

inputs.role: Choice of inertial frame; different frames give different splits.

routes.title: Energy density of the field
routes.formula: u = ½(ε₀|E|² + |B|²/μ₀).

inputs.role: The quadratic form, now with its magnetic part.

routes.title: Force from the Maxwell stress
routes.formula: F = ∮σ·dA over a surface enclosing the charges (minus the change of field momentum inside, added after 1900).

inputs.role: Fields on a surface surrounding the charges.
Rate of change of field momentum inside.

routes.title: Retarded potentials
routes.formula: φ(x,t) = (1/4πε₀)∫ρ(x′, t − |x − x′|/c)/|x − x′| d³x′, and likewise for A.

inputs.role: Lorenz gauge decouples the equations into □φ = ρ/ε₀, □A = μ₀J.

routes.title: Gauge orbit of a pair
routes.formula: All pairs related by gauge transformations form one class.

inputs.role: A scalar potential, now allowed to depend on time.

routes.title: Existence of potentials
routes.formula: Fields obeying ∇·B = 0 and Faraday's law come from some (φ, A), at least locally.

inputs.role: The fields and their two homogeneous equations.
Closed implies exact on regions without holes.

routes.title: Pick a representative
routes.formula: A gauge condition selects a concrete A from the class.

routes.title: Poynting vector
routes.formula: S = E×B/μ₀.

inputs.role: Identifies it as the energy flux in the conservation law.

routes.title: Mode expansion of free fields
routes.formula: Source-free solutions as sums of plane waves.

routes.title: Read off wave data
routes.formula: Each mode has definite k, ω = c|k| and polarization.

inputs.role: Labels modes by wave vector and polarization.

routes.title: Momentum density
routes.formula: g = S/c².

inputs.role: Converts energy flux into momentum density.

routes.title: Lorentz force law
routes.formula: F = q(E + v×B).

inputs.role: Builds the magnetic part q v×B, perpendicular to v.
Adds the electric and magnetic parts.

routes.title: Larmor formula
routes.formula: P = q²a²/(6πε₀c³) for slow charges.

inputs.role: Liénard–Wiechert potentials of the moving charge.
Far-field part of the retarded solution.

routes.title: Flux of the Poynting vector
routes.formula: P = ∮S·dA over a large sphere.

inputs.role: Energy flux far from the charge.
Integrates the flux over the sphere.

routes.title: Assemble the four-potential
routes.formula: (φ/c, A) transform together as a four-vector.

routes.title: Assemble the four-current
routes.formula: J^μ = (cρ, J).

inputs.role: They transform together as a four-vector.

routes.title: Antisymmetrized derivative of A
routes.formula: F_μν = ∂_μA_ν − ∂_νA_μ (Minkowski).

inputs.role: Guarantees the result transforms as a tensor.

routes.title: Contract the field tensor
routes.formula: F_μνF^μν ∝ |B|² − |E|²/c² and F_μνF̃^μν ∝ E·B.

inputs.role: Full contractions are unchanged by every boost and rotation.

routes.title: Stress–energy tensor
